headline: NVIDIA Open-Sourced Linux GPU Kernel Modules to simplify integration and maintenance
summary: NVIDIA open-sourced its Linux GPU kernel modules to simplify integration and maintenance for distributions, enabled by a redesigned driver architecture with GSP firmware. This move aims to reduce operational costs for AI and cloud deployments on Linux.
details: NVIDIA open-sourced its Linux GPU kernel modules to simplify integration, distribution, and maintenance. This strategic move allows distributions to more easily package and update drivers while protecting NVIDIA's core intellectual property.

The open-sourced components are specifically the Linux kernel modules. User-space components like CUDA, OpenGL, Vulkan, and the GSP firmware, which handles critical hardware tasks, remain proprietary.

Previously, NVIDIA's proprietary kernel modules caused issues with DKMS workflows, leading to problems after kernel updates. Open-sourcing simplifies integration for distributions like Ubuntu and Red Hat, streamlining packaging, signing, and updates.

The key technical enabler was the GPU System Processor (GSP) firmware. GSP now manages hardware initialization and control, allowing NVIDIA to expose only the Linux-facing kernel interface as open source.

This was not merely a policy shift; NVIDIA redesigned its driver architecture specifically to enable this. This approach reduces operational costs for deploying AI and cloud infrastructure on Linux, where GPU driver integration is crucial.

The open modules also introduce support for technologies like HMM and Confidential Computing, and are mandatory on newer platforms like Grace Hopper and Blackwell. This provides a clear business advantage for NVIDIA in enterprise environments.

The move also benefits Nouveau, the existing open-source NVIDIA driver, by providing reference code and allowing it to utilize the same GSP firmware for improved power and clock management. The code is dual-licensed MIT/GPLv2, practical for NVIDIA's shared codebase across multiple operating systems.

However, NVIDIA's open kernel modules have not been fully merged into the upstream Linux kernel. This is due to the driver codebase being shared across multiple operating systems and not conforming to Linux kernel upstream coding conventions.

headline_marked: [[Chaos Ransomware in Under 17 Hours]] via Teams IT Support Scam
headline: Chaos Ransomware in Under 17 Hours via Teams IT Support Scam
summary: Attackers are deploying Chaos Ransomware in less than 17 hours by posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams, gaining remote control and encrypting devices.
details: An attacker leverages an external Teams account to impersonate IT support, tricking users into granting remote control. This rapid compromise leads to lateral movement and simultaneous encryption in under 17 hours.

Initial contact is made through an external Microsoft 365 tenant. The attackers use legitimate remote support tools on the victim's device, deploying PowerShell, custom loaders, multiple RMM tools, and a SOCKS tunnel.

The C2 infrastructure operates on attacker web servers, Workers.dev, and dedicated domains. Attackers establish persistent remote control, command execution, an internal proxy, and RDP for lateral movement, culminating in data theft and widespread encryption.
The attack results in readme.chaos.txt files, causing business interruption and double extortion. Manufacturing, energy, construction, and legal services are frequently targeted industries.
Organizations using external Teams federation and Quick Assist should review their security controls and audits. Attackers are actively abusing these legitimate tools for rapid compromise.
